Title: Rome in World Time, Part 7: From the Year of Four Emperors to Marcus Aurelius (AD 69–180)

Summary: Rome's "golden age" began with a civil war, the burning of the Capitol and the destruction of Jerusalem's Temple, and ended with plague and war on the Danube. In between came Vesuvius, the Colosseum, Trajan's conquests to the Persian Gulf, Hadrian's Wall and two more Jewish revolts. At the same time a Chinese envoy tried to reach Rome, paper was presented to the Han court, the Kushan Empire flourished, and a group claiming to be Roman envoys reached China in 166.

---

The second century AD is often called the height of the Roman Empire. Edward Gibbon famously said that if you had to pick the happiest period in human history, you would pick the years from Nerva to Marcus Aurelius (96–180). This post covers that era and the bloody year that came before it.

## The Year of the Four Emperors (AD 69)

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| 15 Jan 69 | **Galba** is murdered in the Forum by Praetorians who back **Otho** |
| Jan 69 | The Rhine legions had already proclaimed their governor **Vitellius** |
| Apr 69 | First Battle of **Bedriacum**: Vitellius' army wins; Otho kills himself |
| 1 Jul 69 | The eastern legions proclaim **Vespasian**, commander in the Jewish War, at Alexandria |
| Oct 69 | Second Battle of Bedriacum; Vespasian's Danube legions sack **Cremona** for four days |
| Dec 69 | Fighting in Rome; the Temple of Jupiter on the Capitol burns; Vitellius is dragged through the streets and killed |

### The Batavian revolt and the "Gallic Empire" (69–70)

During the chaos, **Julius Civilis**, a Batavian (from the Rhine delta) officer in Roman service, revolted. He was joined by Gallic leaders **Classicus**, **Tutor** and **Sabinus**, who proclaimed an "Empire of the Gauls." Astonishingly, several Roman legions on the Rhine surrendered and swore allegiance to it. **Petillius Cerialis** crushed the revolt in 70.

## The Flavians (69–96)

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| **70** | **Titus** takes **Jerusalem** after a five-month siege (August); the Second Temple is burned. Its treasures are later shown on the Arch of Titus |
| 73 or 74 | **Masada** falls; Josephus says the 960 defenders killed themselves first |
| c. 70–80 | The **Colosseum** (Flavian Amphitheatre) is built; opens with 100 days of games in 80 |
| 77–84 | Agricola conquers northern Britain; 83/84 **Mons Graupius** in Scotland |
| **79** | **Vesuvius** buries Pompeii and Herculaneum. Pliny the Elder dies trying to rescue people |
| 80 | Another great fire in Rome |
| 85–89 | Domitian's **Dacian Wars**: the Dacian king **Decebalus** kills a Roman governor and then a Praetorian Prefect; Rome eventually makes a deal |
| **89** | **Revolt of Saturninus**: the governor of Upper Germany rebels at Mainz with two legions, counting on German allies who are stopped by a thawing Rhine |
| 93–96 | Domitian's "reign of terror" against senators |
| 96 | Domitian is murdered in a palace plot (18 September) |

## The "Five Good Emperors" (96–180)

### Nerva (96–98)

The elderly senator **Nerva** was chosen. In 97 the **Praetorian Guard mutinied**, held him hostage and forced him to hand over Domitian's killers. Weakened, Nerva adopted the popular general **Trajan**, which began the system of adoptive succession.

### Trajan (98–117): the empire at its largest

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| 101–102 | First Dacian War |
| 105–106 | Second Dacian War. Decebalus kills himself; **Dacia** becomes a province. The gold captured funds Trajan's Forum and Column |
| 106 | **Nabataea** is annexed as Arabia Petraea |
| 113 | Trajan's Column is dedicated |
| 114–117 | **Parthian War**: Rome annexes Armenia and Mesopotamia, takes the Parthian capital **Ctesiphon** (116) and reaches the Persian Gulf |
| **115–117** | **Kitos War**: Jewish communities in Cyrene, Egypt, Cyprus and Mesopotamia revolt; huge loss of life on all sides |
| 116–117 | Revolts in the newly conquered Mesopotamian cities |
| 117 | Trajan dies in Cilicia. The empire is at its largest extent, about 5 million km² |

### Hadrian (117–138): pulling back and building walls

- 117: Hadrian **gives up Mesopotamia and Armenia** immediately.
- 118: four senior senators are executed for an alleged plot.
- 122: **Hadrian's Wall** is begun across northern Britain.
- 121–125 and 128–132: Hadrian tours nearly the whole empire.
- 130: his companion **Antinous** drowns in the Nile; Hadrian founds a city and a cult for him.
- **132–135/136:** the **Bar Kokhba revolt** in Judaea, after Hadrian plans to rebuild Jerusalem as a Roman colony, Aelia Capitolina. **Simon bar Kokhba** rules an independent state for three years. Cassius Dio says 580,000 Jews were killed in battle; Judaea is renamed **Syria Palaestina**.

### Antoninus Pius (138–161)

The quietest reign in Roman history. He never left Italy. In 142 the **Antonine Wall** was built across Scotland (abandoned about 20 years later). There were small revolts in Mauretania, Britain and Egypt.

### Marcus Aurelius (161–180): philosopher at war

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| 161 | Marcus and his adoptive brother **Lucius Verus** become co-emperors |
| 161–166 | **Parthian War**: Vologases IV invades Armenia and Syria. Romans sack **Seleucia** and Ctesiphon (165) |
| 165/166 onward | The returning army brings the **Antonine Plague** (probably smallpox). Estimates of the death toll range widely, from about 2% to over 10% of the empire's population |
| 166/167–180 | **Marcomannic Wars** on the Danube against the Marcomanni, Quadi and Sarmatians |
| 170 | Germanic tribes break through, besiege **Aquileia** and enter Italy for the first time in nearly 300 years. The Costoboci raid as far as Eleusis in Greece |
| c. 172 | The **Bucoli revolt** in Egypt, led by a priest named Isidorus, nearly takes Alexandria |
| c. 172 | The "Rain Miracle" saves a Roman army from thirst (shown on the Column of Marcus Aurelius) |
| **175** | **Avidius Cassius**, governor of Syria, proclaims himself emperor after a false rumour of Marcus' death. He is killed by his own officers after three months |
| 177 | Persecution of Christians at **Lyon** |
| 180 | Marcus dies on campaign (17 March), probably at Vindobona (Vienna) or Sirmium. His *Meditations*, written in camp, survive |

## Meanwhile, around the world

| Date | Where | What happened | Rome at that moment |
|---|---|---|---|
| 73–102 | Central Asia | Han general **Ban Chao** brings the Tarim Basin back under Chinese control | Flavians, Trajan |
| c. 1st–2nd c. | Mexico | **Teotihuacan**'s Pyramid of the Sun and Pyramid of the Moon are built; the city reaches perhaps 100,000 people | |
| 89–91 | Mongolia | Han general Dou Xian smashes the Northern Xiongnu | **Revolt of Saturninus** |
| **97** | Central Asia | Ban Chao sends **Gan Ying** to reach "Da Qin" (Rome). He reaches the coast of the Persian Gulf (or possibly the Black Sea or the Mediterranean) and turns back when Parthians warn him the voyage could take two years | **Praetorians force Nerva to adopt Trajan** |
| **105** | China | The eunuch **Cai Lun** presents paper made from bark, hemp and rags to the emperor | **Second Dacian War** |
| 107 | Japan | A king of Wa sends 160 slaves as tribute to the Han court | Trajan's Forum under construction |
| c. 106–130 (disputed) | India | Satavahana king Gautamiputra Satakarni defeats the Western Satraps | Trajan |
| c. 127 (disputed) | India/Central Asia | **Kanishka** becomes Kushan emperor; Gandhara Buddhist art flourishes, often with Greco-Roman styles | Hadrian |
| **132** | China | **Zhang Heng** builds a seismoscope that detects distant earthquakes | **Bar Kokhba revolt** begins |
| c. 135 | Caucasus | The Alans raid Roman Cappadocia and are driven off by its governor, the historian Arrian | |
| c. 150 | India | Rudradaman's Junagadh inscription, an early long Sanskrit text in stone | Antoninus Pius |
| c. 150 | Egypt | **Ptolemy** writes the *Almagest*, the astronomy textbook used for 1,400 years | Antoninus Pius |
| 2nd c. | Vietnam | Roman coins of Antoninus Pius and Marcus Aurelius reach the port of **Óc Eo** (Funan kingdom) | |
| c. 150 | Guatemala | **El Mirador** is largely abandoned; Tikal and others will take over | |
| 162 onward | Rome | **Galen** practises medicine in Rome | Parthian war |
| **166** | China | The *Hou Hanshu* records an "embassy" from **Andun**, king of Da Qin (probably Antoninus or Marcus Aurelius), arriving via Rinan (central Vietnam) with ivory and rhinoceros horn | **Antonine Plague** begins |
| 166–169 | China | The Partisan Prohibitions: eunuchs purge scholar-officials at the Han court | Marcomannic invasions |
| late 2nd c. | Eastern Europe | The **Goths** begin moving from the Baltic toward the Black Sea | Marcomannic Wars |
| 2nd c. | Africa | **Aksum** grows into a trading power on the Red Sea | |

## Things you might not have known happened at the same time

**Rome and China almost met in 97, and "met" in 166.** Gan Ying was the furthest-travelling Chinese envoy of antiquity, and he was turned back just as Trajan was about to become emperor. In 166 people claiming to represent the Roman emperor reached Luoyang. Most historians think they were merchants who made the most of the title.

**Paper and the Second Dacian War: 105.** While Trajan was building his famous bridge over the Danube, a Han official was presenting the court with a new writing material. Paper would not reach the Mediterranean world in quantity until the Islamic period, roughly 700 years later.

**The Antonine Plague and Han's troubles may be linked.** Han China suffered serious epidemics in the 160s–180s as well. Some historians suggest the same disease moved across Eurasia along the trade routes, but this is unproven.

**Teotihuacan was booming.** While Hadrian was building his villa at Tivoli, Teotihuacan in the Valley of Mexico was one of the largest cities on Earth, laid out on a grid around its huge pyramids.

**Roman art reached Afghanistan.** Gandharan Buddhist sculptures from Kanishka's empire show the Buddha in draped robes that look like a Roman toga, with Greco-Roman style faces. Trade and artisans moved between the two empires.

## What comes next

Part 8: Commodus the gladiator emperor, the auction of the empire, the Severans, universal citizenship, and the near-collapse of the Third Century, with an emperor captured by Persia and the empire split into three. Meanwhile, China's Han dynasty falls into the Three Kingdoms, and a Japanese queen named Himiko sends envoys to China.

## Sources and notes

- Tacitus, *Histories* (69–70); Suetonius, *Galba* to *Domitian*.
- Josephus, *The Jewish War*, Books 6–7.
- Pliny the Younger, *Letters* 6.16 and 6.20 (Vesuvius) and 10.96–97 (letters with Trajan about Christians).
- Cassius Dio, *Roman History*, Books 64–72 (partly surviving only in later summaries).
- *Historia Augusta* (lives of Hadrian to Marcus). Use with caution; it mixes fact and invention.
- Marcus Aurelius, *Meditations*.
- Fan Ye, *Hou Hanshu*, "Account of the Western Regions," for Gan Ying and the 166 embassy.
- Kyle Harper, *The Fate of Rome* (2017), for the Antonine Plague and climate.
- Overview: [Year of the Four Emperors (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Year_of_the_Four_Emperors), [Bar Kokhba revolt (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bar_Kokhba_revolt), [Sino-Roman relations (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sino-Roman_relations).

**Flags:** The date of the Vesuvius eruption is traditionally 24 August 79, but a charcoal inscription found in 2018 suggests late October; scholars are still divided. Death tolls for the Antonine Plague and the Bar Kokhba revolt are uncertain. Kanishka's accession date has been debated for a century; c. 127 is the current majority view. Cai Lun is credited with paper in official histories, but earlier paper fragments exist, so he improved it rather than inventing it.
